title: Ὠγυγίης λόγος καὶ εὐνή
titleEn: The Tale of Ogygia and a Bed for the Night — Odyssey 7.240–347
part: The Tale of Ogygia and a Bed for the Night (7.240–347)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Asked by Arete where he found the clothes he wears and how he came to the island, Odysseus tells his own story in brief. He was held for seven years on Ogygia by the goddess Calypso, who offered him immortality and never won his heart; in the eighth year she sent him off on a raft with a fair wind. Poseidon wrecked the raft within sight of the Phaeacian coast, and after a hard swim he reached a river mouth and slept in the leaves. There he met Nausicaa and her attendants, and she gave him food, a bath in the river, and the clothes. Alcinous finds fault with his daughter for not bringing the stranger home, but Odysseus defends her. The king then wishes that such a man might stay and marry his daughter, promises a ship for the next day, and boasts of Phaeacian seamanship. Odysseus prays that it may all come true; the queen has beds made under the portico, and the guest lies down to sleep.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’: in Homer the old article is a pronoun. ἀπαμειβόμενος is the present middle participle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, and πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ is built on μῆτις, ‘cunning intelligence’. The whole line is the formula for a man replying to a woman; it introduces Odysseus’s answer to the queen’s questions at the end of the last part. At 302 the same line returns with τὸν ‘him’.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον, βασίλεια, διηνεκέως ἀγορεῦσαι
κήδε’, ἐπεί μοι πολλὰ δόσαν θεοὶ Οὐρανίωνες·
sentences.tr:
argaleon, basileia, diēnekeōs agoreusai
kēde’, epei moi polla dosan theoi Ouraniōnes·
sentences.l:
“Hard, queen, continuously to tell
sorrows, since to me many the gods gave, the children-of-Heaven;
sentences.i: “It is hard, my queen, to tell my sorrows straight through, since the gods, the children of Heaven, gave me so many;
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον is neuter, ‘hard’, with ἐστί left out, and it takes the infinitive ἀγορεῦσαι ‘to tell’; διηνεκέως means ‘from start to finish’. κήδε’ is κήδεα elided, object of the infinitive, and πολλά agrees with it. δόσαν is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι, ‘gave’. Οὐρανίωνες is either ‘descendants of Uranus’ (Heaven) or ‘dwellers in heaven’; the word does not decide, and ‘children of Heaven’ keeps the first while leaving the second open. Murray prints no quotation marks, so the speech begins here without any sign in the Greek.

sentences.t: τοῦτο δέ τοι ἐρέω ὅ μ’ ἀνείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς.
sentences.tr: touto de toi ereō ho m’ aneireai ēde metallāis.
sentences.l: but this to you I will tell, which me you ask and inquire after.
sentences.i: But this I will tell you, what you ask me and inquire after.
sentences.n: τοῦτο is the thing he can tell, and ὅ is the neuter relative ‘what’ (not the article), with μ’ for με ‘me’. ἐρέω is the future of εἶπον ‘I will say’. ἀνείρεαι and μεταλλᾷς are both ‘you ask’: ἀνείρεαι is the epic ἀνείρομαι in its uncontracted second-person form, μεταλλᾷς a contracted form of μεταλλάω ‘inquire, ask after’. τοι is σοι ‘to you’, as in Arete’s question τίς τοι τάδε εἵματ’ ἔδωκεν; near the end of the previous part.

sentences.t: Ὠγυγίη τις νῆσος ἀπόπροθεν εἰν ἁλὶ κεῖται·
sentences.tr: Ōgygiē tis nēsos apoprothen ein hali keitai·
sentences.l: An Ogygian island, a certain one, far off in the salt-sea lies;
sentences.i: There is an island, Ogygia, that lies far off in the sea;
sentences.n: Ὠγυγίη is an adjective, ‘Ogygian’, agreeing with νῆσος ‘island’; in English it becomes the island’s name. τις is ‘a certain’. ἀπόπροθεν ‘far off’ carries the suffix -θεν, which properly means ‘from’, so it marks distance. εἰν is ἐν, and ἁλί is the dative of ἅλς ‘sea’; κεῖται is ‘lies’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν Ἄτλαντος θυγάτηρ, δολόεσσα Καλυψὼ
ναίει ἐυπλόκαμος, δεινὴ θεός·
sentences.tr:
entha men Atlantos thygatēr, doloessa Kalypsō
naiei eyplokamos, deinē theos·
sentences.l:
There indeed, Atlas’ daughter, guileful Calypso,
dwells, fine-plaited, the dread goddess;
sentences.i: There dwells Atlas’s daughter, guileful Calypso, fine-plaited, the dread goddess;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘there’, and μέν looks ahead to the contrast that ἀλλά opens at 248. δολόεσσα is the feminine of δολόεις ‘guileful’, from δόλος ‘trick’. ἐυπλόκαμος ‘fine-plaited’ is her standing epithet, of her hair; δεινὴ θεός is ‘the dread goddess’, δεινός here meaning awe-inspiring rather than merely frightening. ναίει is ‘dwells’, and the two-word phrase Ἄτλαντος θυγάτηρ is ‘daughter of Atlas’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις αὐτῇ
μίσγεται οὔτε θεῶν οὔτε θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr:
oude tis autēi
misgetai oute theōn oute thnētōn anthrōpōn.
sentences.l:
and not any with her
mingles, neither of gods nor of mortal men.
sentences.i: and no one keeps company with her, neither among gods nor among mortal men.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τις is ‘and no one’. μίσγεται is the epic form of μίγνυμαι, ‘mixes with, has dealings with’, with αὐτῇ ‘with her’. θεῶν and ἀνθρώπων are partitive genitives depending on τις, in the pair οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’: no one among either race. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia that ends the last one.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ τὸν δύστηνον ἐφέστιον ἤγαγε δαίμων
οἶον, ἐπεί μοι νῆα θοὴν ἀργῆτι κεραυνῷ
Ζεὺς ἔλσας ἐκέασσε μέσῳ ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ.
sentences.tr:
all’ eme ton dystēnon ephestion ēgage daimōn
oion, epei moi nēa thoēn argēti keraunōi
Zeus elsas ekeasse mesōi eni oinopi pontōi.
sentences.l:
But me, the wretched one, to her hearth brought a power,
alone, when to me my swift ship with the bright thunderbolt
Zeus, having pinned it, shattered in the middle of the wine-faced open-sea.
sentences.i: But some power brought me, the wretched one, alone to her hearth, after Zeus had pinned down my swift ship with the bright thunderbolt and shattered it in the middle of the sea that has the look of wine.
sentences.n: ἀλλά answers the μέν of 245: she lives alone, but I was brought to her. ἐφέστιον is an adjective ‘at the hearth’ agreeing with ἐμέ; the hearth was where a stranger took refuge. δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, not one particular god. οἶον is ‘alone’. ἔλσας, from εἴλω, means ‘having pinned’ (shut in and pressed); ἐκέασσε is the aorist of κεάζω ‘split, shatter’. ἀργῆτι κεραυνῷ is ‘with the bright thunderbolt’, and οἴνοπι is the adjective οἶνοψ, ‘wine-faced’. Line 250 is word for word a line spoken earlier about the same wreck.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἀπέφθιθεν ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τρόπιν ἀγκὰς ἑλὼν νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης
ἐννῆμαρ φερόμην·
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi men pantes apephthithen esthloi hetairoi,
autar egō tropin ankas helōn neos amphielissēs
ennēmar pheromēn·
sentences.i: There all the others perished, my good companions, but I took the keel of the ship curved on both sides in my arms and was carried along for nine days;
sentences.n: ἀπέφθιθεν is the aorist passive of ἀποφθίνω ‘perish’, with the epic ending -θεν for -θησαν. αὐτάρ is the epic ‘but’. ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, ‘having taken’, and ἀγκάς means ‘in the arms’, so he clasps the keel. ἀμφιελίσσης, agreeing with νεός ‘of the ship’, is an old epithet whose sense is disputed: ‘curved on both sides’ or ‘rowed on both sides’. ἐννῆμαρ ‘for nine days’ is an adverb made from ἐννέα and ἦμαρ; φερόμην is the passive ‘I was carried’.

sentences.t:
δεκάτῃ δέ με νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ
νῆσον ἐς Ὠγυγίην πέλασαν θεοί, ἔνθα Καλυψὼ
ναίει ἐυπλόκαμος, δεινὴ θεός,
sentences.tr:
dekatēi de me nykti melainēi
nēson es Ōgygiēn pelasan theoi, entha Kalypsō
naiei eyplokamos, deinē theos,
sentences.l:
and on the tenth, black night, me
to the Ogygian island brought-near the gods, where Calypso
dwells, fine-plaited, the dread goddess,
sentences.i: and on the tenth, dark night, the gods brought me near to the island of Ogygia, where Calypso dwells, fine-plaited, the dread goddess,
sentences.n: δεκάτῃ is dative of the time ‘on the tenth’; the noun νυκτί ‘night’ follows, with μελαίνῃ ‘black’. πέλασαν is an unaugmented aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’, and the subject θεοί is left to the end. ἔνθα here is ‘where’. The words ἔνθα Καλυψὼ ναίει ἐυπλόκαμος, δεινὴ θεός nearly repeat 245–246, so the English repeats too. The unit stops at a comma because the relative clause that follows would otherwise run to five lines.

sentences.t:
ἥ με λαβοῦσα
ἐνδυκέως ἐφίλει τε καὶ ἔτρεφεν ἠδὲ ἔφασκε
θήσειν ἀθάνατον καὶ ἀγήραον ἤματα πάντα·
sentences.tr:
hē me labousa
endykeōs ephilei te kai etrephen ēde ephaske
thēsein athanaton kai agēraon ēmata panta·
sentences.i: She took me and kindly loved and nurtured me, and kept telling me that she would make me immortal and ageless for all my days;
sentences.n: ἥ is the relative ‘who’ (feminine, Calypso), and λαβοῦσα is the aorist participle of λαμβάνω, ‘having taken’. ἐφίλει and ἔτρεφεν are imperfects, ‘she loved’ and ‘she nurtured’. ἔφασκε is an iterative imperfect of φημί, with the suffix -σκ- meaning ‘she used to say, kept saying’. θήσειν is the future infinitive of τίθημι, ‘that she would make’. ἤματα πάντα is ‘all my days’, and the line repeats one already heard about the same offer.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμὸν οὔ ποτε θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔπειθεν.
sentences.tr: all’ emon ou pote thymon eni stēthessin epeithen.
sentences.l: but my heart never in my breast did she persuade.
sentences.i: but she never persuaded the heart in my breast.
sentences.n: ἐμὸν is the possessive adjective ‘my’, agreeing with θυμόν. ἐνί is ἐν, and στήθεσσιν is a dative in -εσσι(ν): ‘in my breast’, the plural standing for one chest. ἔπειθεν is an imperfect, so it says she was always trying and never won him over.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν ἑπτάετες μένον ἔμπεδον, εἵματα δ’ αἰεὶ
δάκρυσι δεύεσκον, τά μοι ἄμβροτα δῶκε Καλυψώ·
sentences.tr:
entha men heptaetes menon empedon, heimata d’ aiei
dakrysi deueskon, ta moi ambrota dōke Kalypsō·
sentences.l:
There indeed for seven years I stayed on steadily, and the clothes always
with tears I kept wetting, which to me, deathless, gave Calypso;
sentences.i: There I stayed on steadily for seven years, and kept wetting with tears the deathless clothes that Calypso gave me;
sentences.n: ἑπτάετες ‘for seven years’ is an adverb made from ἑπτά and ἔτος; ἔμπεδον is ‘steadily, without moving’. δεύεσκον is another iterative imperfect in -σκ-, ‘I kept wetting’, from δεύω. δάκρυσι is a dative plural, ‘with tears’. τά is the relative ‘which’, and ἄμβροτα ‘deathless’ agrees with εἵματα, the clothes; δῶκε is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι. These are the clothes Calypso gave him; the set he is wearing now came from Nausicaa, as 296 says.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ὀγδόατόν μοι ἐπιπλόμενον ἔτος ἦλθεν,
καὶ τότε δή μ’ ἐκέλευσεν ἐποτρύνουσα νέεσθαι
Ζηνὸς ὑπ’ ἀγγελίης, ἢ καὶ νόος ἐτράπετ’ αὐτῆς.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē ogdoaton moi epiplomenon etos ēlthen,
kai tote dē m’ ekeleusen epotrynousa neesthai
Zēnos hyp’ angeliēs, ē kai noos etrapet’ autēs.
sentences.l:
But when indeed the eighth for me, coming-round, year came,
and then indeed me she bade, urging me, to go
at the message of Zeus, or her own mind was turned.
sentences.i: But when the eighth year came round for me, then she bade me, urging me on, to go, either at a message from Zeus or because her own mind had turned.
sentences.n: ὀγδόατον is the epic form of ὄγδοον ‘eighth’, and ἐπιπλόμενον is the participle of ἐπιπέλομαι, said of a year that ‘comes round’. ἐκέλευσεν … νέεσθαι is ‘she bade me go’, νέεσθαι the uncontracted infinitive. ὑπ’ ἀγγελίης means ‘at the prompting of a message’, Ζηνός being the genitive of Ζεύς. ἢ καί introduces the second possibility, and ἐτράπετ’ is the aorist middle of τρέπω, ‘was turned’. Odysseus offers both explanations without choosing.

sentences.t:
πέμπε δ’ ἐπὶ σχεδίης πολυδέσμου, πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκε,
σῖτον καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ, καὶ ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕσσεν,
οὖρον δὲ προέηκεν ἀπήμονά τε λιαρόν τε.
sentences.tr:
pempe d’ epi schediēs polydesmou, polla d’ edōke,
siton kai methy hēdy, kai ambrota heimata hessen,
ouron de proeēken apēmona te liaron te.
sentences.l:
And she sent me on a raft of many bonds, and much she gave,
food and sweet wine, and deathless clothes she clothed me in,
and a fair wind she sent forth, harmless and warm.
sentences.i: She sent me off on a raft of many lashings and gave me much, food and sweet wine; she clothed me in deathless clothes, and sent a fair wind ahead of me, harmless and warm.
sentences.n: πέμπε is an imperfect, ‘was sending’. σχεδίης πολυδέσμου is a genitive after ἐπί, ‘on a raft of many bonds’, the bonds being the lashings that hold the logs together. πολλά is ‘many things’, and σῖτον καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ ‘food and sweet wine’ names them; μέθυ is a poetic neuter word for wine. ἕσσεν, from ἕννυμι, takes two accusatives, the clothes and the person; only ἄμβροτα εἵματα stands in the Greek and ‘me’ is understood: she put deathless clothes on him. προέηκεν is the aorist of προίημι ‘send forth’. Line 266 is a repeat of a line spoken in the narrator’s own account of the same departure.

sentences.t:
ἑπτὰ δὲ καὶ δέκα μὲν πλέον ἤματα ποντοπορεύων,
ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῃ δ’ ἐφάνη ὄρεα σκιόεντα
γαίης ὑμετέρης, γήθησε δέ μοι φίλον ἦτορ
δυσμόρῳ·
sentences.tr:
hepta de kai deka men pleon ēmata pontoporeuōn,
oktōkaidekatēi d’ ephanē orea skioenta
gaiēs hymeterēs, gēthēse de moi philon ētor
dysmorōi·
sentences.l:
Seven and ten days I sailed, crossing the open sea,
and on the eighteenth appeared the shadowy mountains
of your land, and rejoiced, for me, my dear heart,
ill-fated;
sentences.i: For seventeen days I sailed, crossing the open sea, and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains of your land came into view, and my heart rejoiced, ill-fated man that I was;
sentences.n: πλέον is the first-person imperfect ‘I sailed’, uncontracted and without augment; the narrator’s account of the same voyage has the third-person πλέεν ‘he sailed’, and otherwise the same first two lines. ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῃ is dative of time, ‘on the eighteenth’. ὄρεα is the uncontracted plural of ὄρος. γαίης ὑμετέρης is ‘of your land’, and ὑμετέρης is a plural ‘your’, of the Phaeacians as a people. μοι … δυσμόρῳ is ‘to me, ill-fated’: the dative of the person, with the adjective agreeing. The unit ends at the ano teleia inside line 270.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ ἔμελλον ἔτι ξυνέσεσθαι ὀιζυῖ
πολλῇ, τήν μοι ἐπῶρσε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων,
sentences.tr:
ē gar emellon eti xynesesthai oizui
pollēi, tēn moi epōrse Poseidaōn enosichthōn,
sentences.l:
for indeed I was still about to be joined with misery
much, which upon me had stirred Poseidon the earth-shaker,
sentences.i: for I was still to be joined with much misery, which Poseidon the earth-shaker had stirred up against me,
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’. ἔμελλον with a future infinitive is ‘I was about to, I was destined to’, and ξυνέσεσθαι is the future infinitive of σύνειμι, ‘be with’, taking the dative ὀιζυῖ ‘misery’; πολλῇ agrees with it. τήν is the relative ‘which’, and ἐπῶρσε is the aorist of ἐπόρνυμι, ‘stirred up upon’, with μοι ‘against me’. Ποσειδάων is the epic form of Ποσειδῶν. The unit stops at the comma because the next relative clause would carry it past four lines.

sentences.t:
ὅς μοι ἐφορμήσας ἀνέμους κατέδησε κέλευθον,
ὤρινεν δὲ θάλασσαν ἀθέσφατον, οὐδέ τι κῦμα
εἴα ἐπὶ σχεδίης ἁδινὰ στενάχοντα φέρεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hos moi ephormēsas anemous katedēse keleuthon,
ōrinen de thalassan athesphaton, oude ti kyma
eia epi schediēs hadina stenachonta pheresthai.
sentences.l:
who, against me having set the winds, bound my path,
and stirred the sea, immense, and not any wave
allowed upon the raft, thickly groaning, to be carried.
sentences.i: He set the winds upon me and blocked my path, and stirred up the immense sea, and no wave would let me be carried on the raft as I groaned heavily.
sentences.n: ὅς is the relative, ‘who’, still Poseidon. ἐφορμήσας is ‘having set upon’, and κατέδησε ‘bound down’ says the winds barred his way. ἀθέσφατον is ‘immense’; the word’s origin is uncertain (perhaps ‘beyond what can be declared’). In the last line κῦμα is the subject of εἴα, the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’; ‘me’ is understood as the object, and στενάχοντα agrees with it. ἁδινά is an adverb, ‘thickly, heavily’. So the waves kept him from riding the raft in peace.

sentences.t: τὴν μὲν ἔπειτα θύελλα διεσκέδασ’·
sentences.tr: tēn men epeita thyella dieskedas’·
sentences.l: That one, then, a storm-blast scattered;
sentences.i: Then a storm-blast scattered it;
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘it’, the raft (σχεδίης, feminine, in 274); it is the pronoun, not the article. θύελλα is the subject, and διεσκέδασ’ is the aorist of διασκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’, elided. The μέν here is answered by the αὐτάρ that opens the next unit, which begins in the same line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε
νηχόμενος τόδε λαῖτμα διέτμαγον, ὄφρα με γαίῃ
ὑμετέρῃ ἐπέλασσε φέρων ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
autar egō ge
nēchomenos tode laitma dietmagon, ophra me gaiēi
hymeterēi epelasse pherōn anemos te kai hydōr.
sentences.l:
but I, for my part,
swimming, this gulf cut-through, until me to your land
brought-near, carrying me, both wind and water.
sentences.i: but I, for my part, swimming, cut my way across this gulf, until wind and water carried me and brought me to your land.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε is ‘but I, for my part’, the γε stressing the contrast with the raft. νηχόμενος is the present participle of νήχομαι ‘swim’. διέτμαγον is a second aorist of διατμήγω, ‘I cut through’, and λαῖτμα is the gulf or deep of the sea. ὄφρα … ἐπέλασσε is ‘until … brought near’, with φέρων ‘carrying’ agreeing with ἄνεμος. ὑμετέρῃ is again the plural ‘your’, as in 269.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κέ μ’ ἐκβαίνοντα βιήσατο κῦμ’ ἐπὶ χέρσου,
πέτρῃς πρὸς μεγάλῃσι βαλὸν καὶ ἀτερπέι χώρῳ·
sentences.tr:
entha ke m’ ekbainonta biēsato kym’ epi chersou,
petrēis pros megalēisi balon kai aterpei chōrōi·
sentences.l:
There would me, as I came out, have overpowered a wave on the dry land,
having hurled me against great rocks and a joyless place;
sentences.i: There, as I came out on the dry land, a wave would have overpowered me, dashing me against great rocks and a joyless place;
sentences.n: κε with an aorist indicative (βιήσατο) says what would have happened but did not: ‘would have overpowered’. ἐκβαίνοντα is the participle ‘as I came out’, and ἐπὶ χέρσου is ‘on the dry land’. βαλόν is the aorist participle of βάλλω, neuter to agree with κῦμα: the wave ‘having thrown me’. πέτρῃς … μεγάλῃσι is a dative in -ῃσι, ‘against great rocks’, and ἀτερπέι ‘joyless’ belongs with χώρῳ ‘place’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἀναχασσάμενος νῆχον πάλιν, ἧος ἐπῆλθον
ἐς ποταμόν, τῇ δή μοι ἐείσατο χῶρος ἄριστος,
λεῖος πετράων, καὶ ἐπὶ σκέπας ἦν ἀνέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
all’ anachassamenos nēchon palin, hēos epēlthon
es potamon, tēi dē moi eeisato chōros aristos,
leios petraōn, kai epi skepas ēn anemoio.
sentences.l:
But, having drawn back, I swam again, until I came
to a river, where indeed to me it seemed the best place,
smooth of rocks, and where there was shelter from the wind.
sentences.i: But I drew back and swam on again, until I came to a river, at the place that seemed to me best, free of rocks and sheltered from the wind.
sentences.n: ἀναχασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’. ἧος is the epic ἕως ‘until’. ἐείσατο is the aorist of εἴδομαι, ‘seemed’, with μοι ‘to me’, and χῶρος is ‘place’. πετράων is a genitive of separation, ‘smooth of rocks’, so ‘free of rocks’. καὶ ἐπὶ σκέπας ἦν is ‘and there was shelter besides’, with ἐπί standing apart from ἦν (tmesis) and ἀνέμοιο a genitive in -οιο. The last line repeats one heard earlier.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἔπεσον θυμηγερέων, ἐπὶ δ’ ἀμβροσίη νὺξ
ἤλυθ’.
sentences.tr:
ek d’ epeson thymēgereōn, epi d’ ambrosiē nyx
ēlyth’.
sentences.l:
And out I fell, spirit-gathering, and upon me ambrosial night
came.
sentences.i: I dropped out of the water, gathering my spirits, and ambrosial night came on.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἔπεσον is tmesis for ἐξέπεσον, ‘fell out’ of the water. θυμηγερέων is the participle of a compound of θυμός ‘spirit’ and ἀγείρω ‘gather’, ‘gathering my spirit’, with uncontracted -έων; the exact sense is not certain (recovering himself, in some way), so both layers keep the parts. ἀμβροσίη is the ‘deathless’ word usually said of the gods’ food, here applied to the night. ἐπί … ἤλυθ’ is again tmesis, ‘came on’, and ἤλυθ’ is ἤλυθε, the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι. The sentence ends at a full stop inside line 284.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἀπάνευθε διιπετέος ποταμοῖο
ἐκβὰς ἐν θάμνοισι κατέδραθον, ἀμφὶ δὲ φύλλα
ἠφυσάμην·
sentences.tr:
egō d’ apaneuthe diipeteos potamoio
ekbas en thamnoisi katedrathon, amphi de phylla
ēphysamēn·
sentences.i: And I climbed out some way from the river fallen from Zeus, and lay down to sleep among the bushes, and heaped leaves around me;
sentences.n: ἀπάνευθε is ‘apart from, away from’, with the genitive ποταμοῖο. διιπετέος is an old epithet of rivers, usually explained as ‘fallen from Zeus’, that is fed by rain; the meaning is not certain, so the English keeps the literal parts. ἐκβάς is the aorist participle of ἐκβαίνω. κατέδραθον, the aorist of καταδαρθάνω, means ‘I lay down to sleep’. ἀμφὶ … ἠφυσάμην is ‘I drew up around myself’: ἀφύσσω is ‘draw, scoop’, so he heaped the leaves about him.

sentences.t: ὕπνον δὲ θεὸς κατ’ ἀπείρονα χεῦεν.
sentences.tr: hypnon de theos kat’ apeirona cheuen.
sentences.l: and sleep a god poured down, boundless.
sentences.i: and a god poured boundless sleep down upon me.
sentences.n: κατ’ … χεῦεν is tmesis, ‘poured down’, with χεῦεν the unaugmented aorist of χέω. ἀπείρονα ‘boundless’ agrees with ὕπνον. The god is not named. ὕπνον is accusative, object of the verb, and θεός is the subject.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν ἐν φύλλοισι φίλον τετιημένος ἦτορ
εὗδον παννύχιος καὶ ἐπ’ ἠῶ καὶ μέσον ἦμαρ.
sentences.tr:
entha men en phylloisi philon tetiēmenos ētor
heudon pannychios kai ep’ ēō kai meson ēmar.
sentences.l:
There indeed among the leaves, grieved in my dear heart,
I slept, all night long and toward dawn and the middle day.
sentences.i: There among the leaves, grieving in my heart, I slept all night, and on toward dawn, and up to midday.
sentences.n: τετιημένος is a perfect participle meaning ‘grieved, troubled’, and φίλον ἦτορ is an accusative of respect, ‘as to his dear heart’. εὗδον is ‘I slept’, without augment. παννύχιος is an adjective used like an adverb, ‘all night long’. ἐπ’ ἠῶ is ἐπὶ ἠῶ, ‘on toward dawn’ (ἠώς, accusative), and μέσον ἦμαρ ‘the middle day’ is midday. Odysseus tells how long he slept, which fits the exhaustion of the last swim.

sentences.t: δείλετό τ’ ἠέλιος καί με γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἀνῆκεν.
sentences.tr: deileto t’ ēelios kai me glykys hypnos anēken.
sentences.l: And the sun declined, and me sweet sleep released.
sentences.i: The sun began to sink, and sweet sleep let me go.
sentences.n: δείλετο is a past tense of δείλομαι, ‘turn toward evening’ (imperfect or aorist; the tense is not certain), from δείλη ‘late afternoon’, so the sun was already declining when he woke. ἠέλιος is the epic form of ἥλιος. ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι, ‘let go, released’, with με as its object.

sentences.t:
ἀμφιπόλους δ’ ἐπὶ θινὶ τεῆς ἐνόησα θυγατρὸς
παιζούσας, ἐν δ’ αὐτὴ ἔην ἐικυῖα θεῇσι·
sentences.tr:
amphipolous d’ epi thini teēs enoēsa thygatros
paizousas, en d’ autē eēn eikuia theēisi·
sentences.l:
And attendants on the shore of your daughter I perceived
playing, and among them herself was, like to goddesses;
sentences.i: I saw your daughter’s attendants playing on the shore, and she herself among them, like goddesses;
sentences.n: ἀμφιπόλους is ‘attendants’ (women who wait on someone), and ἐνόησα is the aorist of νοέω ‘perceive’. θινί is the dative of θίς ‘shore’. τεῆς is the Homeric form of σῆς ‘your’, the possessive of the second person, agreeing with θυγατρός. ἐν δ’ is ‘and among them’, the preposition standing alone, and ἔην is the epic imperfect ἦν. ἐικυῖα θεῇσι ‘like to goddesses’ has the dative in -ῃσι.

sentences.t: τὴν ἱκέτευσ’·
sentences.tr: tēn hiketeus’·
sentences.l: Her I supplicated;
sentences.i: I made my plea to her as a suppliant;
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’ (accusative), the pronoun. ἱκέτευσ’ is ἱκέτευσα, ‘I approached as a suppliant’: the word for the ritual plea of a stranger who has no claim but need. The unit is one clause, and it ends at the ano teleia inside line 292.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ οὔ τι νοήματος ἤμβροτεν ἐσθλοῦ,
ὡς οὐκ ἂν ἔλποιο νεώτερον ἀντιάσαντα
ἐρξέμεν·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ou ti noēmatos ēmbroten esthlou,
hōs ouk an elpoio neōteron antiasanta
erxemen·
sentences.i: and she did not fail in good sense, as you would not expect a younger person to act on meeting you;
sentences.n: ἡ is the article as a pronoun, ‘she’. ἤμβροτεν is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’, and νοήματος ἐσθλοῦ is the genitive it governs, ‘a good thought’: she did not miss it. ὡς οὐκ ἂν ἔλποιο is ‘as you would not expect’, with ἄν and the optative in a general second person. ἀντιάσαντα is the aorist participle of ἀντιάω ‘meet’, agreeing with νεώτερον ‘a younger person’. ἐρξέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, the future infinitive of ἔρδω ‘do’ (= ἔρξειν), the tense that ἔλποιο ‘expect’ takes.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ γάρ τε νεώτεροι ἀφραδέουσιν.
sentences.tr: aiei gar te neōteroi aphradeousin.
sentences.l: for always, indeed, younger people are thoughtless.
sentences.i: for the young are always thoughtless.
sentences.n: αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί, ‘always’. γάρ τε is ‘for’ with the epic τε that marks a general truth, and the comparative νεώτεροι is used without a comparison, ‘the younger’, that is the young as a class. ἀφραδέουσιν is the uncontracted third-person plural of ἀφραδέω ‘be thoughtless’ (Attic ἀφραδοῦσιν). Odysseus’s remark also softens what he has just said: Nausicaa did well for one so young.

sentences.t:
ἥ μοι σῖτον ἔδωκεν ἅλις ἠδ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον
καὶ λοῦσ’ ἐν ποταμῷ καί μοι τάδε εἵματ’ ἔδωκε.
sentences.tr:
hē moi siton edōken halis ēd’ aithopa oinon
kai lous’ en potamōi kai moi tade heimat’ edōke.
sentences.l:
She to me food gave in plenty and the fire-faced wine,
and bathed me in the river, and to me these clothes gave.
sentences.i: She gave me food in plenty and the wine that has the look of fire, and bathed me in the river, and gave me these clothes.
sentences.n: ἥ is again ‘she’, Nausicaa. ἅλις is ‘in plenty’, and αἴθοπα οἶνον is ‘fire-faced wine’, like οἶνοψ ‘wine-faced’ of the sea. λοῦσ’ is elided and could be λοῦσα ‘I bathed’ or λοῦσε ‘she bathed’; the English takes the second. The active aorist of λούω is transitive (bathing oneself is the middle), the subject ἥ runs on unchanged from ἔδωκεν, with μοι of that clause serving as the object ‘me’, and the line is a list of what Nausicaa did for him; the first reading would change the subject with no pronoun to say so. τάδε εἵματ’ is ‘these clothes’, the words of Arete’s own question earlier in the scene, and this line answers it: the clothes he wears came from Nausicaa.

sentences.t: ταῦτά τοι ἀχνύμενός περ ἀληθείην κατέλεξα.
sentences.tr: tauta toi achnymenos per alētheiēn katelexa.
sentences.l: These things to you, grieving though I be, in truth I have recounted.”
sentences.i: I have told you all this truthfully, though it grieves me.”
sentences.n: ταῦτα is ‘these things’, and τοι is σοι, ‘to you’. ἀχνύμενός περ is ‘although grieving’: περ makes a participle concessive. ἀληθείην, ‘truth’, is an Ionic form (Attic ἀλήθειαν) used adverbially, ‘truthfully’. κατέλεξα is the aorist of καταλέγω ‘recount, tell in order’. The line closes Odysseus’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Alkinoos apameibeto phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Alcinous, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, the pronoun. δ’ αὖτ’ is δὲ αὖτε ‘and in turn’, and ἀπαμείβετο is the imperfect middle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’. φώνησεν is the aorist of φωνέω ‘speak, raise the voice’, with -τε ‘and’ attached. The line is the formula for Alcinous answering, and 308 repeats it.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἦ τοι μὲν τοῦτό γ’ ἐναίσιμον οὐκ ἐνόησε
παῖς ἐμή, οὕνεκά σ’ οὔ τι μετ’ ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶν
ἦγεν ἐς ἡμέτερον, σὺ δ’ ἄρα πρώτην ἱκέτευσας.
sentences.tr:
xein’, ē toi men touto g’ enaisimon ouk enoēse
pais emē, houneka s’ ou ti met’ amphipoloisi gynaixin
ēgen es hēmeteron, sy d’ ara prōtēn hiketeusas.
sentences.l:
“Stranger, truly this, at least, of what is fitting my child
did not think of, in that you not at all with her attendant women
she led to our house, though you first supplicated her.”
sentences.i: “Stranger, in this at least my child did not think of what is fitting, in that she did not bring you to our house with her attendant women, though it was to her that you first made your plea.”
sentences.n: ἦ τοι μέν is an emphatic ‘truly’. ἐναίσιμον is ‘fitting, in due measure’, and οὐκ ἐνόησε is ‘did not think of, did not have in mind’. οὕνεκα is ‘in that, because’, giving the fault. ἦγεν ἐς ἡμέτερον is ‘led to ours’, with δόμον ‘house’ understood. πρώτην is feminine because it agrees with the ‘her’ that ἱκέτευσας ‘you supplicated’ leaves unspoken. Alcinous takes Odysseus’s account as it stands and finds only the girl at fault.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: The line is the masculine of 240, and the English is the same except for ‘him’. τὸν is the pronoun, ἀπαμειβόμενος is the participle ‘answering’, and προσέφη is ‘addressed’. It again marks a reply from a man to a man.

sentences.t: ἥρως, μή τοι τοὔνεκ’ ἀμύμονα νείκεε κούρην·
sentences.tr: hērōs, mē toi tounek’ amymona neikee kourēn·
sentences.l: “Hero, do not, for that reason, the blameless girl rebuke;
sentences.i: “Hero, do not rebuke the blameless girl on that account;
sentences.n: ἥρως is ‘hero’ used as a title of respect. μή with the imperative νείκεε, from νεικέω ‘rebuke, quarrel with’, is ‘do not rebuke’. τοι is either the particle ‘I tell you’ or σοι ‘to you’, and the light force is carried by the imperative alone. τοὔνεκ’ is τοῦ ἕνεκα ‘for that reason’, with crasis and elision. ἀμύμονα is ‘blameless’, the stock epithet, translated the same each time; here it is Odysseus’s defence of her.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν γάρ μ’ ἐκέλευε σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισιν ἕπεσθαι,
ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἔθελον δείσας αἰσχυνόμενός τε,
μή πως καὶ σοὶ θυμὸς ἐπισκύσσαιτο ἰδόντι·
sentences.tr:
hē men gar m’ ekeleue syn amphipoloisin hepesthai,
all’ egō ouk ethelon deisas aischynomenos te,
mē pōs kai soi thymos episkyssaito idonti·
sentences.i: For she did bid me follow with her attendants, but I was unwilling, from fear and shame, lest your heart too should be angered at the sight;
sentences.n: ἡ is ‘she’, the article as a pronoun, and ἐκέλευε and ἔθελον are imperfects, ‘she was bidding’ and ‘I was unwilling’. δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’, and αἰσχυνόμενος is ‘feeling shame’. μή πως with the optative ἐπισκύσσαιτο is ‘lest in some way … grow angry’, a fear after a past verb. σοί … ἰδόντι is a dative and its participle, ‘to you, seeing it’: your heart, at the sight. καὶ σοί is ‘to you too’, you as well as any man, which the general truth of the next line explains.

sentences.t: δύσζηλοι γάρ τ’ εἰμὲν ἐπὶ χθονὶ φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr: dyszēloi gar t’ eimen epi chthoni phyl’ anthrōpōn.
sentences.l: for jealous indeed are we upon the earth, the tribes of men.”
sentences.i: for we tribes of men upon the earth are jealous.”
sentences.n: δύσζηλοι is ‘jealous’, a compound of δυσ- ‘ill’ and ζῆλος; it means quick to suspect and resent, not merely envious. εἰμέν is the epic first-person plural ‘we are’ (Attic ἐσμέν). γάρ τε is ‘for’ with the epic τε of a general truth. φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων is ‘tribes of men’, φῦλα elided, in apposition to the ‘we’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Alkinoos apameibeto phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Alcinous, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: This is the formula of 298 again, with the same English: ἀπαμείβετο ‘answered’ and φώνησεν ‘spoke’, τὸν the pronoun ‘him’.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, οὔ μοι τοιοῦτον ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλον κῆρ
μαψιδίως κεχολῶσθαι·
sentences.tr:
xein’, ou moi toiouton eni stēthessi philon kēr
mapsidiōs kecholōsthai·
sentences.l:
“Stranger, not to me such in my breast a dear heart
is, without cause to be angered;
sentences.i: “Stranger, the heart in my breast is not such as to be angry without cause;
sentences.n: κῆρ is ‘heart’, a different word from ἦτορ and θυμός; φίλον is ‘dear’, and ἐστί is left out. τοιοῦτον means ‘of such a kind’, and the infinitive κεχολῶσθαι, the perfect passive of χολόω ‘to be angry’, completes it: not of such a kind as to be angry. μαψιδίως is ‘idly, without reason’. οὔ μοι is ‘not in my case’, with the dative of the person. ἐνὶ στήθεσσι is ‘in the breast’, the dative in -εσσι.

sentences.t: ἀμείνω δ’ αἴσιμα πάντα.
sentences.tr: ameinō d’ aisima panta.
sentences.l: but better are all things done in due measure.
sentences.i: and better is everything done in due measure.
sentences.n: ἀμείνω is the neuter plural of ἀμείνων ‘better’ (contracted from ἀμείνονα). αἴσιμα is ‘in due measure, fitting’, from αἶσα ‘portion’, and it is a different word from ἐναίσιμον in 299 only by its prefix. The line is a proverb: moderation in all things is better than anger. It ends Alcinous’s first reason for not being angry.

sentences.t:
αἲ γάρ, Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον,
τοῖος ἐὼν οἷός ἐσσι, τά τε φρονέων ἅ τ’ ἐγώ περ,
παῖδά τ’ ἐμὴν ἐχέμεν καὶ ἐμὸς γαμβρὸς καλέεσθαι
αὖθι μένων·
sentences.tr:
ai gar, Zeu te pater kai Athēnaiē kai Apollon,
toios eōn hoios essi, ta te phroneōn ha t’ egō per,
paida t’ emēn echemen kai emos gambros kaleesthai
authi menōn·
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
such being as you are, and thinking the very things I think,
my child to have, and my son-in-law to be called,
here remaining;
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — you, being the man you are and thinking the very things I think, might have my daughter and be called my son-in-law, staying on here;
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ, ‘would that’, opens a wish, and in the wish the infinitives ἐχέμεν ‘to have’ and καλέεσθαι ‘to be called’ stand for ‘you might have … be called’. ἐχέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, and καλέεσθαι is uncontracted (Attic καλεῖσθαι). ἐών is ὤν, ἐσσί is ‘you are’, and τοῖος … οἷος is ‘such as’; τά … ἅ is ‘the things that’, with περ ‘the very’. γαμβρός is a relative by marriage, here ‘son-in-law’. To ‘have’ a child here means to marry her. This is a marriage offer, and the three gods are invoked over it. αὖθι is ‘right here’, and μένων ‘staying’ goes with it: to stay on here.

sentences.t:
οἶκον δέ κ’ ἐγὼ καὶ κτήματα δοίην,
εἴ κ’ ἐθέλων γε μένοις·
sentences.tr:
oikon de k’ egō kai ktēmata doiēn,
ei k’ ethelōn ge menois·
sentences.l:
and a house and possessions I would give,
if willingly you would stay;
sentences.i: and I would give you a house and possessions, if you would stay willingly;
sentences.n: δοίην is the aorist optative of δίδωμι, ‘I would give’, with κε; εἴ κε with the optative μένοις is ‘if you would stay’. ἐθέλων is ‘willing’, so the offer stands only if he chooses it. κτήματα are ‘possessions’. The unit begins in mid-line, with οἶκον, and stops at the next ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀέκοντα δέ σ’ οὔ τις ἐρύξει
Φαιήκων·
sentences.tr:
aekonta de s’ ou tis eryxei
Phaiēkōn·
sentences.l:
but unwilling you no one will hold back
of the Phaeacians;
sentences.i: but no one of the Phaeacians will keep you here against your will;
sentences.n: ἀέκοντα is ‘unwilling’, accusative, agreeing with σ’ (σε); ἀέκων is the epic form of ἄκων. ἐρύξει is the future of ἐρύκω ‘hold back, detain’. Φαιήκων is the partitive genitive after οὔ τις: no one among the Phaeacians. The speaker hedges the offer, keeping hospitality free of force.

sentences.t: μὴ τοῦτο φίλον Διὶ πατρὶ γένοιτο.
sentences.tr: mē touto philon Dii patri genoito.
sentences.l: not this dear to Father Zeus may it be.
sentences.i: may that never be pleasing to Father Zeus.
sentences.n: μή with the optative γένοιτο is a wish against something: ‘may it not happen’. φίλον Διὶ πατρί is ‘dear to Father Zeus’, φίλον predicate and Διί the dative of the person. τοῦτο is what was just said, the holding of a guest against his will; the line works like ‘Zeus forbid’.

sentences.t:
πομπὴν δ’ ἐς τόδ’ ἐγὼ τεκμαίρομαι, ὄφρ’ ἐὺ εἰδῇς,
αὔριον ἔς·
sentences.tr:
pompēn d’ es tod’ egō tekmairomai, ophr’ ey eidēis,
aurion es·
sentences.l:
And an escort, for this I fix, that you may know it well:
for tomorrow;
sentences.i: I fix your escort for tomorrow, so that you may know it well;
sentences.n: πομπήν is ‘escort’, the conveyance home that a host gives a guest. τεκμαίρομαι is ‘I fix, I appoint’, from τέκμαρ ‘sign, fixed mark’. ἐς τόδ’ … αὔριον ἔς is ‘for this … for tomorrow’: τόδε points forward to the day. ὄφρ’ ἐὺ εἰδῇς is ‘so that you may know well’, with εἰδῇς the subjunctive of οἶδα, and ἐὺ = εὖ. The unit ends at the ano teleia inside line 318.

sentences.t:
τῆμος δὲ σὺ μὲν δεδμημένος ὕπνῳ
λέξεαι, οἱ δ’ ἐλόωσι γαλήνην, ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκηαι
πατρίδα σὴν καὶ δῶμα, καὶ εἴ πού τοι φίλον ἐστίν,
sentences.tr:
tēmos de sy men dedmēmenos hypnōi
lexeai, hoi d’ eloōsi galēnēn, ophr’ an hikēai
patrida sēn kai dōma, kai ei pou toi philon estin,
sentences.l:
and then you, overcome by sleep,
will lie down, and they will row over the calm, until you come
to your fatherland and house, and wherever it is dear to you,
sentences.i: And then you, overcome by sleep, will lie down while they row over the calm water, until you reach your fatherland and house, or wherever else is dear to you,
sentences.n: τῆμος is ‘then’, that is, on the day just named. δεδμημένος is the perfect participle of δάμνημι, ‘overcome’, with ὕπνῳ ‘by sleep’; λέξεαι is the uncontracted future of λέγομαι ‘lie down’. ἐλόωσι is ‘they will drive’, uncontracted, and γαλήνη is the calm of the sea. ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκηαι is ‘until you come’, ἵκηαι a subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι. πατρίδα σήν is ‘your fatherland’, and καὶ εἴ πού τοι φίλον ἐστίν is ‘and if anywhere is dear to you’: he may go elsewhere, even farther.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ καὶ μάλα πολλὸν ἑκαστέρω ἔστ’ Εὐβοίης,
τήν περ τηλοτάτω φάσ’ ἔμμεναι, οἵ μιν ἴδοντο
λαῶν ἡμετέρων, ὅτε τε ξανθὸν Ῥαδάμανθυν
ἦγον ἐποψόμενον Τιτυὸν Γαιήιον υἱόν.
sentences.tr:
ei per kai mala pollon hekasterō est’ Euboiēs,
tēn per tēlotatō phas’ emmenai, hoi min idonto
laōn hēmeterōn, hote te xanthon Rhadamanthyn
ēgon epopsomenon Tityon Gaiēion huion.
sentences.l:
even if very much farther it is than Euboea,
which furthest they say it is, those who saw it
of our people, when fair-haired Rhadamanthys
they led to look upon Tityus, Earth’s son.
sentences.i: even if it is very much farther than Euboea, which those of our people who saw it say is the farthest of all, when they led fair-haired Rhadamanthys to see Tityus, the son of Earth.
sentences.n: ἑκαστέρω is the comparative adverb ‘farther’, with the genitive Εὐβοίης ‘than Euboea’. τήν, feminine, is Euboea; φάσ’ is φάσι ‘they say’, and τηλοτάτω is the superlative ‘farthest’, with ἔμμεναι the epic infinitive of εἰμί. οἵ … ἴδοντο is ‘those who saw’ (the middle aorist without augment), with the partitive λαῶν ἡμετέρων ‘of our people’. ὅτε τε is ‘when’. ἦγον is ‘they were leading’, and ἐποψόμενον is a future participle, ‘to look upon’, expressing purpose. Γαιήιον is ‘of Gaia’ (Earth). Alcinous gives a story only as a measure of distance.

sentences.t:
καὶ μὲν οἱ ἔνθ’ ἦλθον καὶ ἄτερ καμάτοιο τέλεσσαν
ἤματι τῷ αὐτῷ καὶ ἀπήνυσαν οἴκαδ’ ὀπίσσω.
sentences.tr:
kai men hoi enth’ ēlthon kai ater kamatoio telessan
ēmati tōi autōi kai apēnysan oikad’ opissō.
sentences.l:
And indeed they went there, and without toil accomplished it
on that same day, and completed it, home back again.
sentences.i: And indeed they went there and, without toil, accomplished it on that same day, and came back home again.
sentences.n: οἱ is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, the Phaeacians of the tale. τέλεσσαν is an aorist with doubled σ, ‘they accomplished’, and ἄτερ καμάτοιο is ‘without toil’ (ἄτερ takes the genitive). ἤματι τῷ αὐτῷ is ‘on that same day’, in the dative of time. ἀπήνυσαν is the aorist of ἀνύω, ‘finish’, with ὀπίσσω ‘back’; οἴκαδ’ is οἴκαδε, ‘homeward’, with the suffix -δε. So the round trip took a single day.

sentences.t:
εἰδήσεις δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ὅσσον ἄρισται
νῆες ἐμαὶ καὶ κοῦροι ἀναρρίπτειν ἅλα πηδῷ.
sentences.tr:
eidēseis de kai autos eni phresin hosson aristai
nēes emai kai kouroi anarriptein hala pēdōi.
sentences.l:
and you will know for yourself in your mind how much the best
are my ships and my young men at tossing up the salt-sea with the oar-blade.”
sentences.i: And you will find out for yourself, in your own mind, how much the best my ships and young men are at tossing up the salt sea with the oar.”
sentences.n: εἰδήσεις is the future of οἶδα, ‘you will know’, and ἐνὶ φρεσί is ‘in your mind’. ὅσσον ἄρισται is ‘how much the best they are’, ἄρισται the superlative, feminine plural, agreeing with νῆες and standing for κοῦροι too. κοῦροι are ‘young men’. ἀναρρίπτειν is ‘to throw up’, and ἅλα is the accusative of ἅλς ‘salt-sea’. πηδῷ is a dative ‘with the oar-blade’ (πηδόν), used of the oars as a whole. The unit closes Alcinous’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δὲ πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
εὐχόμενος δ’ ἄρα εἶπεν, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, gēthēsen de polytlas dios Odysseus,
euchomenos d’ ara eipen, epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rejoiced much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
and praying then he said, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus rejoiced, and, praying, he spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’, and γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’; πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’. εὐχόμενος is ‘praying’; εὔχομαι can also mean ‘declare, boast’, and here it is prayer. The last words are a formula, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν, ‘spoke a word and called him by name’, with ἐκ … ὀνόμαζεν in tmesis; the name that follows is Zeus’s.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, αἴθ’ ὅσα εἶπε τελευτήσειεν ἅπαντα
Ἀλκίνοος·
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater, aith’ hosa eipe teleutēseien hapanta
Alkinoos·
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, would that whatever he has said he might bring to fulfilment, all of it,
Alcinous;
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, if only Alcinous might bring to pass all that he has said;
sentences.n: αἴθε is ‘would that’, a second wish-word, like αἲ γάρ in 311. ὅσα εἶπε is ‘as many things as he said’, and ἅπαντα ‘all of it’ stresses that none should fail. τελευτήσειεν is the aorist optative of τελευτάω ‘bring to an end, fulfil’, the subject Ἀλκίνοος being held to the next line. The unit ends at the ano teleia inside line 332.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μέν κεν ἐπὶ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν
ἄσβεστον κλέος εἴη, ἐγὼ δέ κε πατρίδ’ ἱκοίμην.
sentences.tr:
tou men ken epi zeidōron arouran
asbeston kleos eiē, egō de ke patrid’ hikoimēn.
sentences.l:
of him indeed would upon the grain-giving plough-land
fame unquenchable be, and I would come to my fatherland.”
sentences.i: then his fame would never go out over the grain-giving plough-land, and I would reach my own fatherland.”
sentences.n: τοῦ μέν is ‘of him indeed’, the genitive of possession with κλέος ‘fame’, answered by ἐγὼ δέ ‘but I’. κεν with εἴη and ἱκοίμην gives ‘would be’ and ‘would come’, the results if the wish came true. ἐπὶ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν is ‘over the grain-giving plough-land’; ζείδωρος is usually ‘grain-giving’, though ‘life-giving’ was also proposed. ἄσβεστον ‘unquenchable’ is literally ‘that cannot be put out’, as of fire. πατρίδ’ is πατρίδα, ‘fatherland’, and ἱκοίμην is the aorist optative of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon·
sentences.l: So they, such things to one another were saying;
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another;
sentences.n: ὣς is the adverb ‘so’; οἱ μέν is ‘they, for their part’, with the article as pronoun, and μέν looks ahead to what the women do next. τοιαῦτα is ‘such things’, and πρὸς ἀλλήλους is ‘to one another’. ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω, ‘were saying’. The line closes the talk and opens a new paragraph in the text.

sentences.t:
κέκλετο δ’ Ἀρήτη λευκώλενος ἀμφιπόλοισιν
δέμνι’ ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ θέμεναι καὶ ῥήγεα καλὰ
πορφύρε’ ἐμβαλέειν, στορέσαι τ’ ἐφύπερθε τάπητας
χλαίνας τ’ ἐνθέμεναι οὔλας καθύπερθεν ἕσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
kekleto d’ Arētē leukōlenos amphipoloisin
demni’ hyp’ aithousēi themenai kai rhēgea kala
porphyre’ embaleein, storesai t’ ephyperthe tapētas
chlainas t’ enthemenai oulas kathyperthen hesasthai.
sentences.l:
And ordered Arete, white-armed, her attendants
bedsteads under the portico to place, and fine blankets,
purple, to throw on, and to spread carpets over them,
and to put in thick cloaks, to wear as covering on top.
sentences.i: White-armed Arete gave orders to her attendants to place bedsteads under the portico, throw fine purple blankets on them, spread carpets over the top, and put in thick cloaks to serve as covering on top.
sentences.n: κέκλετο is an aorist middle of κέλομαι, ‘she called out orders’, and ἀμφιπόλοισιν is the dative ‘to her attendants’, with Ἀρήτη λευκώλενος ‘white-armed Arete’ as subject. θέμεναι, ἐμβαλέειν, στορέσαι and ἐνθέμεναι are infinitives after κέκλετο: θέμεναι is the epic form of θεῖναι, and ἐμβαλέειν is the uncontracted ἐμβαλεῖν. δέμνια are the bedsteads, ῥήγεα blankets, and αἴθουσα is the roofed portico of the house. πορφύρε’ is πορφύρεα, ‘purple’. ἕσασθαι is ‘to clothe oneself’, that is to serve as a covering.

sentences.t: αἱ δ’ ἴσαν ἐκ μεγάροιο δάος μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσαι·
sentences.tr: hai d’ isan ek megaroio daos meta chersin echousai·
sentences.l: And they went out of the hall, torches in their hands holding;
sentences.i: And they went out of the hall, holding torches in their hands;
sentences.n: αἱ is ‘they’, the attendants, the article as a pronoun. ἴσαν is the epic third-person plural imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. ἐκ μεγάροιο is ‘out of the hall’, with the genitive in -οιο, and δάος is a torch. ἔχουσαι is the feminine participle ‘holding’. The line ends at an ano teleia: their going out is complete, and the next unit shows the work.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ στόρεσαν πυκινὸν λέχος ἐγκονέουσαι,
ὤτρυνον δ’ Ὀδυσῆα παριστάμεναι ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei storesan pykinon lechos enkoneousai,
ōtrynon d’ Odysēa paristamenai epeessin·
sentences.l:
But when they had spread the solid bed, bustling about,
they urged on Odysseus, standing beside him, with words:
sentences.i: But when they had made up the solid bed, working with speed, they urged Odysseus on with words, standing beside him:
sentences.n: στόρεσαν is the unaugmented aorist of στορέννυμι ‘spread’, and πυκινὸν λέχος is ‘the solid bed’. ἐγκονέουσαι is the feminine participle of ἐγκονέω, ‘bustling, hurrying’. ὤτρυνον is the imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’. Ὀδυσῆα is a metrical variant of Ὀδυσσῆα (in both spellings the accusative), and παριστάμεναι is ‘standing beside him’. ἐπέεσσιν is the dative ‘with words’, in -εσσι(ν).

sentences.t: ὄρσο κέων, ὦ ξεῖνε·
sentences.tr: orso keōn, ō xeine·
sentences.l: “Arise, to lie down, stranger;
sentences.i: “Up, stranger, and go to bed;
sentences.n: ὄρσο is the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse yourself, get up’. κέων is a participle of an old verb ‘go to bed’, related to κεῖμαι ‘lie’, giving the purpose: ‘get up to lie down’. ὦ ξεῖνε is ‘stranger’ as an address. The Greek has no quotation marks, so the maids’ words begin here without any sign; the first half of the line stops at an ano teleia.

sentences.t: πεποίηται δέ τοι εὐνή.
sentences.tr: pepoiētai de toi eunē.
sentences.l: and made ready for you is the couch.”
sentences.i: and your couch is made.”
sentences.n: πεποίηται is the perfect passive of ποιέω, ‘has been made’, the perfect giving a finished state. τοι is σοι, ‘for you’, dative of the person, and δέ is ‘and’. εὐνή is ‘couch’, the bed as it is laid out, in contrast to δέμνια, the bedsteads above. The last words of the maids close their brief speech.

sentences.t: ὣς φάν, τῷ δ’ ἀσπαστὸν ἐείσατο κοιμηθῆναι.
sentences.tr: hōs phan, tōi d’ aspaston eeisato koimēthēnai.
sentences.l: So they spoke, and to him welcome it seemed to sleep.
sentences.i: So they spoke, and to him it seemed welcome to go to sleep.
sentences.n: φάν is the third-person plural of φημί (= ἔφασαν), ‘they spoke’, without augment. τῷ is ‘to him’, the pronoun. ἐείσατο is the aorist of εἴδομαι ‘seemed’, used impersonally with the dative, and ἀσπαστόν is ‘welcome’, the thing longed for. κοιμηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of κοιμάω, ‘to go to sleep’. His long day is over.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν ἔνθα καθεῦδε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
τρητοῖς ἐν λεχέεσσιν ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ἐριδούπῳ·
sentences.tr:
hōs ho men entha katheude polytlas dios Odysseus
trētois en lecheessin hyp’ aithousēi eridoupōi·
sentences.l:
So he indeed there was sleeping, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
on a bored bedstead beneath the loud-echoing portico;
sentences.i: So much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus lay sleeping there, on a corded bedstead under the loud-echoing portico;
sentences.n: ὣς ὁ μὲν is ‘so he, for his part’, with ὁ ‘he’ and μέν answered by the δέ of the next unit. καθεῦδε is the imperfect ‘was sleeping’, without augment. τρητοῖς ἐν λεχέεσσιν is ‘on a bored bedstead’: the frame was pierced with holes for the cords (or thongs) that supported the bedding. λεχέεσσιν is a dative in -εσσι(ν), plural for one bed. ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ ἐριδούπῳ is ‘under the loud-echoing portico’, ἐρίδουπος being ‘loud-sounding’.

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίνοος δ’ ἄρα λέκτο μυχῷ δόμου ὑψηλοῖο,
πὰρ δὲ γυνὴ δέσποινα λέχος πόρσυνε καὶ εὐνήν.
sentences.tr:
Alkinoos d’ ara lekto mychōi domou hypsēloio,
par de gynē despoina lechos porsyne kai eunēn.
sentences.l:
And Alcinous then lay down in the innermost part of the high house,
and beside him the woman, the lady, made ready bed and couch.
sentences.i: Alcinous lay down in the innermost part of the high house, and beside him his wife, the lady of the house, made ready the bed and couch.
sentences.n: λέκτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of λέγομαι, ‘lay down’. μυχῷ is a dative of place, ‘in the innermost part’, and δόμου ὑψηλοῖο is ‘of the high house’, the genitive in -οιο. πάρ is παρά ‘beside’, as an adverb. γυνὴ δέσποινα is ‘the woman, the lady’, that is his wife, the lady of the house. πόρσυνε is ‘made ready’, from πορσύνω, with the objects λέχος ‘bed’ and εὐνήν ‘couch’. The part ends with the two of them, king and queen, in bed.
